data.title: Youngest billionaires in America are mostly AI founders
data.ai_summary: Forbes' 2026 400 list shows 10 youngest billionaires, seven of whom are first-time members and all tied to AI. Anthropic cofounders hold four spots, with combined net worth of $169 billion, down from $357 billion in 2025.
data.author: Cris Tolomia

industries.name: Net Worth & Personal Balance Sheet Tracking

data.full_text: 1 / 12 List slides 7 of America's 10 youngest billionaires got rich from AI List slides Previous Start over By · Updated October 22, 2026 Add QZ to Google Manoj Gopanapalli / Unsplash The fastest route into America’s most exclusive financial club now runs through artificial intelligence. Forbes set a record $4.4 billion minimum to qualify for its 2026 Forbes 400 ranking of the country’s richest people. That bar did little to slow a wave of thirtysomething AI founders. A year ago, only four people under 40 had enough money to make the list. This year there are 10. The shift shows up clearly in Forbes’ ranking of the 10 youngest billionaires on the 2026 Forbes 400, which lists the under-40 members from oldest to youngest using net worths as of September 4, 2026. Seven of the 10 are first-time members of the Forbes 400, and Forbes ties every one of those seven fortunes to the AI boom. Anthropic alone accounts for four of the names. The maker of the Claude AI models was started in 2021 by seven people who left OpenAI, worried that their former employer was moving too fast on a powerful technology without enough attention to safety. Each of the four younger cofounders on the list is worth an estimated $15.5 billion. OpenAI supplies the richest newcomer on the entire 2026 ranking. Defense-tech company Anduril and coding startup Cognition supply the two youngest members. Only three people carried over from the 2025 under-40 group: Surge AI founder Edwin Chen, Robinhood cofounder Vlad Tenev and Walmart $WMT heir Lukas Walton. Walton is the only member of the group who inherited his money. The group’s combined wealth fell even as its headcount grew. Forbes puts the total net worth of the 10 youngest at $169 billion, less than half the $357 billion figure from 2025. The drop mostly reflects older and richer moguls aging past 40. The biggest of them is Meta $META cofounder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg, now 42, whose fortune Forbes estimates at $212 billion. Venture capitalist Josh Kushner and Airbnb $ABNB cofounder Nathan Blecharczyk also aged out. The result is a snapshot of where new American wealth is being created fastest. Here are the youngest billionaires in America on the 2026 Forbes 400, listed from oldest to youngest. Lukas Walton, the Walmart heir and richest Forbes 400 member under 40 KDavid Montero / Unsplash Lukas Walton, 39, sits at No. 10 on Forbes’ 2026 list of the youngest Forbes 400 members, with an estimated net worth of $44.4 billion. He is the wealthiest person in the under-40 group and the only one whose fortune was inherited rather than built. Walton’s money traces back to his grandfather, Sam Walton, who opened the first Walmart $WMT in Rogers, Arkansas, in 1962. The company grew into the world’s largest retailer by revenue, and it is still headquartered in nearby Bentonville. Sam Walton died in 1992. His family remains one of the richest in the U.S. because its members still hold a large share of Walmart stock. Lukas is the only child of John Walton, one of Sam’s sons. John died in 2005 when the ultralight aircraft he was flying crashed in Wyoming. According to Forbes, Lukas inherited about a third of his father’s estate, and most of it was Walmart shares. That leaves his net worth closely tied to the retailer’s stock price. Rather than working inside the family business, Walton runs Builders Vision, a Chicago-based firm that combines investing and philanthropy. Forbes reports it manages more than $15 billion. Its focus areas include clean energy, sustainable food systems and ocean conservation. That places Walton in the impact-investing camp, which tries to earn financial returns while pursuing environmental goals. In June 2026, he added a sports asset by buying a minority stake in the NBA’s Chicago Bulls. Jerry Reinsdorf has led the team’s ownership since 1985. The franchise is best known for the six championships it won in the 1990s with Michael Jordan. Walton’s presence on this list draws a contrast with the other nine names. Every other member of the group qualified on the strength of a company he or she started or helped found. Walton’s place reflects inheritance and age instead. His fortune also skews the group’s math. Walton’s estimated $44.4 billion alone represents roughly a quarter of the $169 billion that Forbes says the 10 youngest members hold combined. The next-richest member of the group, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman, is worth less than 60% of that. Vlad Tenev’s Robinhood fortune at 39 appshunter.io / Unsplash Vlad Tenev, 39, ranks No. 9 among the youngest members of the 2026 Forbes 400, with an estimated $7.1 billion fortune. Most of it comes from his roughly 6% stake in Robinhood, the trading app he cofounded in 2013. Tenev was born in Bulgaria to parents who both worked for the World Bank, and he grew up in northern Virginia after the family moved to the U.S. He studied mathematics at Stanford, where he met Baiju Bhatt. Bhatt, now 41, is also a member of the Forbes 400. Robinhood’s original pitch was simple: stock trades with no commission. The idea spread across the brokerage industry. By late 2019, major rivals such as Charles Schwab $SCHW, TD Ameritrade and E*Trade had dropped commissions on online stock trades. The company drew intense scrutiny in January 2021, when it temporarily restricted purchases of GameStop $GME and other heavily traded meme stocks. Tenev testified before Congress about the episode the following month. Robinhood went public on the Nasdaq $NDAQ later in 2021 under the ticker HOOD. Its newest growth engine looks little like its original product. Forbes reports that prediction markets are now Robinhood’s fastest-growing business. Customers use them to trade contracts tied to future events, including elections, Federal Reserve decisions, sports and the weather. In the second quarter of 2026, prediction markets generated more than $156 million in revenue for Robinhood, more than either stock or crypto trading. That shift puts the company at the center of a fast-growing and closely watched corner of finance. Prediction markets let customers bet on real-world outcomes through regulated contracts, and their growth has drawn attention from regulators and from rival platforms. Tenev also has a foothold in AI. In 2023, he founded Harmonic, a startup focused on mathematical reasoning, and he serves as its chair. The venture connects to his academic roots. Tenev left a mathematics doctoral program at UCLA to pursue his first startup with Bhatt. He is one of only three people who were among the 10 youngest Forbes 400 members in 2025 and kept that status in 2026. The other two are Walmart $WMT heir Lukas Walton and Surge AI founder Edwin Chen. Tom Brown, Anthropic cofounder and lead author of the GPT-3 paper Brecht Corbeel / Unsplash Tom Brown, 39, is No. 8 on the list of the youngest 2026 Forbes 400 members, worth an estimated $15.5 billion as an Anthropic cofounder. His career tracks the rise of large language models, from his early work at OpenAI to the computing systems behind Anthropic’s Claude. Brown studied computer science and cognitive science at MIT. He joined OpenAI while it was still a small research lab and was among its first 20 employees, according to Forbes. His best-known contribution came in 2020. Brown was the lead author of “Language Models are Few-Shot Learners,” the paper that introduced GPT-3. The model showed that a large enough language model could write fluent text and handle new tasks from a few examples in a prompt, without being retrained for each one. The paper won a best paper award at NeurIPS, one of the field’s top academic conferences. GPT-3 also laid the groundwork for the products that set off the current wave of AI investment. In 2021, Brown was one of seven OpenAI staffers who left to start Anthropic. At the new company, his responsibility is compute — the vast clusters of specialized chips needed to train and run models like Claude. That job has become one of the most expensive and strategically important in the industry. Anthropic trains and serves its models on hardware from several suppliers, including Google $GOOGL’s tensor processing units, Amazon $AMZN’s Trainium chips and Nvidia $NVDA’s graphics processors. Brown shares his ranking on the broader list with his fellow cofounders. Forbes estimates each of the seven is worth $15.5 billion, which places them in a tie for No. 75 on the full Forbes 400. Those fortunes rest on Anthropic’s private valuation. The company was most recently valued at $965 billion after a $65 billion funding round in May 2026. Forbes also reports that Anthropic confidentially filed this summer to eventually go public, as did OpenAI. That valuation explains how an engineer who left OpenAI in 2021 joined the ranks of the richest Americans five years later. Brown’s wealth comes from early equity in a lab that grew into one of the most valuable private companies in the world. Daniela Amodei, Anthropic president and the youngest list’s only woman Brecht Corbeel / Unsplash Daniela Amodei, 39, is No. 7 on Forbes’ 2026 ranking of the youngest Forbes 400 members, with an estimated $15.5 billion fortune. She cofounded Anthropic and serves as its president, and she is the only woman among the 10 youngest members of this year’s list. Amodei’s path into AI did not start in computer science. She graduated from the University of California, Santa Cruz, and later worked at Stripe, the online payments company, before moving to OpenAI. There, she oversaw safety and policy work, an area that would shape the company she went on to help build. In 2021, she left OpenAI along with her brother, Dario Amodei, and five other colleagues to start Anthropic. Dario, 43, is the company’s CEO. He also joined the Forbes 400 for the first time this year, but his age keeps him off the under-40 list. Two other Anthropic cofounders in their early 40s are also newcomers this year, according to Forbes. Forbes says Daniela Amodei is Anthropic’s president and board chair, with responsibility for research, engineering, product and commercial operations. That puts her in charge of much of the machinery that turns Claude from a research project into a business serving companies and individual users. Anthropic is organized as a public benefit corporation. That legal structure requires its leaders to weigh a stated public mission alongside returns to shareholders. The company has made AI safety central to its identity since its founding, and that emphasis has become part of how it competes with OpenAI, Google $GOOGL and others for customers and researchers. The cofounders have also made a commitment about what happens to their money. Earlier in 2026, Amodei and the other six cofounders pledged to eventually give away 80% of their wealth. At an estimated $15.5 billion each, 80% would come to more than $12 billion per founder at current valuations. On the full 2026 Forbes 400, Amodei shares a tie at No. 75 with her fellow Anthropic cofounders. Edwin Chen, the Surge AI founder who never raised venture money Mika Baumeister / Unsplash Edwin Chen, 38, ranks No. 6 among the youngest members of the 2026 Forbes 400, with an estimated $18 billion fortune. He built it through Surge AI, a company that supplies human-generated data for training AI models, without raising venture capital. Forbes estimates he owns about 75% of it. Chen’s background is a long way from Silicon Valley. He grew up in a Florida town of about 3,400 people, where his parents, immigrants from Taiwan, ran a restaurant serving Chinese and Thai food. He later studied math, linguistics and computer science at MIT, then worked at Google $GOOGL, Facebook $META and Twitter $TWTR. He founded Surge AI in 2020. The company pays people to label data and to rate and correct answers produced by AI systems. That human feedback is a core ingredient in modern model training. Techniques such as reinforcement learning from human feedback, often called RLHF, rely on people judging which responses are better so a model can learn to produce more helpful and accurate output. Surge’s customers include Google and Anthropic, according to Forbes, and the company has passed $1 billion in annual revenue. Reaching that scale without outside venture funding is rare in AI, where many companies raise billions of dollars before they turn a profit. Because Chen did not sell large blocks of equity to investors, he kept a controlling stake. That is why his fortune exceeds those of several founders whose companies carry far higher valuations. Surge competes in a crowded market for AI training data. Its best-known rival, Scale AI, became 49% owned by Meta in 2025. That deal led some AI labs to reconsider sending sensitive training work to a company partly owned by a competitor. Chen is one of three people who were among the 10 youngest Forbes 400 members in 2025 and kept that spot in 2026. He is a returning member rather than a newcomer, but his company sits squarely inside the AI supply chain. Surge earns its money by making other companies’ models better, which ties its fortunes directly to how much the big labs spend on training. Greg Brockman, OpenAI president and the richest Forbes 400 newcomer Levart_Photographer / Unsplash Greg Brockman, 38, is No. 5 among the youngest members of the 2026 Forbes 400 and the richest newcomer on the entire list. Forbes estimates his net worth at $25.5 billion, most of it from his stake in OpenAI, the company he cofounded and serves as president. Brockman grew up in North Dakota and enrolled at both Harvard and MIT without finishing a degree at either. He joined Stripe early and became its chief technology officer at 25. In 2015, he cofounded OpenAI as a nonprofit research lab with Sam Altman and Elon Musk. The size of his stake stayed private until a court case brought it out. Musk sued Brockman and Altman in 2024 over OpenAI’s conversion to a for-profit structure. During the trial in May 2026, Brockman testified under oath that his OpenAI holdings are worth more than $20 billion. He also disclosed nearly $500 million in Stripe stock and smaller positions in chipmaker Cerebras and cloud computing provider CoreWeave. Both companies supply OpenAI. OpenAI’s growth made those numbers possible. The company released ChatGPT in November 2022, and the chatbot became one of the fastest-adopted consumer products ever. OpenAI was valued at $852 billion in March 2026, according to Forbes. Brockman’s tenure has had interruptions. When OpenAI’s board removed Altman as CEO in November 2023, Brockman quit the same day, then returned days later after Altman was reinstated. He also took an extended leave in 2024 before coming back. His role has expanded since then. Brockman has long overseen the infrastructure that runs OpenAI’s models, and in July 2026 he also took charge of the company’s product business. Forbes describes that combination as making him OpenAI’s second-in-command ahead of a possible initial public offering. Brockman’s estimated $25.5 billion makes him the second-richest member of the under-40 group, behind only Walmart $WMT heir Lukas Walton. Among those in the group who built their own fortunes, no one is richer. Jack Clark, the former Bloomberg reporter who cofounded Anthropic Sebastian Schuster / Unsplash Jack Clark, 37, is No. 4 on Forbes’ list of the youngest 2026 Forbes 400 members, with an estimated $15.5 billion fortune as an Anthropic cofounder. A former journalist, he has become one of the AI industry’s most visible voices on public policy. Clark covered artificial intelligence as a reporter for Bloomberg before he moved to the other side of the story. He joined OpenAI as its policy director, working on how governments and the public should respond to increasingly capable AI systems. In 2021, he left OpenAI with six colleagues to found Anthropic. Since then, Forbes notes, he has been one of the sector’s more prominent supporters of government regulation of AI. That stance sets him apart from many technology executives who have resisted new rules. His public profile includes appearances before lawmakers and international bodies. In July 2023, he briefed the United Nations Security Council during its first meeting dedicated to artificial intelligence. Outside Anthropic, Clark is known for Import AI, a weekly newsletter that summarizes and comments on new AI research. It has a wide following among researchers, investors and policymakers. He has also helped lead the AI Index, an annual report published by Stanford’s Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence that tracks progress and trends across the field. Today, Clark runs an in-house think tank at Anthropic that studies how AI affects society. The role extends the work he did as a journalist and policy director: explaining a fast-moving technology to people outside the research labs and shaping the rules that govern it. Like each of Anthropic’s seven cofounders, Clark is estimated to be worth $15.5 billion. He shares the cofounders’ tie at No. 75 on the full 2026 Forbes 400. His path to that ranking is unusual for a billionaire technologist. Clark did not build models or write the company’s code. His fortune comes from cofounder equity in a lab whose valuation climbed into the hundreds of billions of dollars. He is the second-youngest of the four Anthropic cofounders on the under-40 list, behind only Sam McCandlish. Sam McCandlish, the physicist behind Anthropic’s AI scaling work Brecht Corbeel / Unsplash Sam McCandlish, 36, is No. 3 among the youngest members of the 2026 Forbes 400 and the youngest of the four Anthropic cofounders on the list. Forbes estimates his fortune at $15.5 billion. McCandlish trained as a scientist. He earned a Ph.D. in theoretical physics at Stanford before joining OpenAI, where he worked on what are now known as scaling laws. The core finding was that AI models improve in a predictable way as researchers add more training data, larger models and more computing power. That research became one of the most consequential ideas in modern AI. A 2020 OpenAI paper on scaling laws for neural language models listed McCandlish among its authors, alongside future Anthropic cofounder Jared Kaplan. It gave companies a way to forecast the payoff from bigger training runs. The finding helped justify the enormous spending on chips and data centers that now defines the industry. McCandlish had earlier been the lead author of a 2018 OpenAI study on large-batch training. That paper examined how the amount of data processed in each training step affects the efficiency of learning, a practical question for anyone training models at scale. Physics runs through Anthropic’s founding team. Kaplan was a theoretical physics professor at Johns Hopkins University. CEO Dario Amodei earned a Ph.D. in biophysics at Princeton. That shared background helps explain the company’s early focus on measuring and predicting how models behave as they grow. After cofounding Anthropic in 2021, McCandlish served as its chief technology officer. In October 2025, he moved into a new role as chief architect. In that job, he oversees how the company’s models are designed and trained. His estimated $15.5 billion matches that of each of his fellow cofounders. At 36, McCandlish is younger than every other first-time Forbes 400 member except Palmer Luckey and Steven Hao. All three owe their fortunes to companies founded within the past decade. Palmer Luckey, Anduril founder and second-youngest Forbes 400 member Remy Gieling / Unsplash Palmer Luckey, 33, is No. 2 on Forbes’ list of the youngest 2026 Forbes 400 members, with an estimated $5.9 billion fortune from Anduril, the defense technology company he founded in 2017. He is the second-youngest person on the entire list. Luckey’s first fortune came from virtual reality. As a teenager in Southern California, he built prototype headsets in his parents’ garage. The company he started, Oculus, raised about $2.4 million on Kickstarter in 2012. Facebook $META bought Oculus in 2014 for $2 billion in cash and stock when Luckey was 21. He left Facebook , now Meta , in 2017 after controversy over his political support for Donald Trump. That same year, he founded Anduril with cofounders that included former Palantir $PLTR employees and a partner at the venture firm Founders Fund. The name comes from a sword in J.R.R. Tolkien’s “The Lord of the Rings.” Anduril builds autonomous drones and sensors, along with AI-powered software that coordinates them. Its core software platform, Lattice, pulls data from many systems so operators can track and direct them from a single interface. The company is based in Costa Mesa, California. Anduril had a big first half of 2026. In March, the U.S. Army awarded it a 10-year contract for software, hardware and related services worth up to $20 billion. Two months later, the company raised $5 billion from venture investors at a $61 billion valuation. That round pushed Luckey onto the Forbes 400 as a newcomer. Luckey has since mended ties with his former employer. In 2025, Anduril and Meta announced a partnership to develop mixed-reality headsets for the U.S. military, bringing his virtual reality roots and his defense business together. His rise reflects a broader shift in Silicon Valley’s relationship with the Pentagon. A decade ago, many large tech companies kept their distance from military work. Anduril built its business around it, betting that cheaper autonomous systems and software would win contracts long dominated by traditional defense contractors such as Lockheed Martin $LMT and Northrop Grumman $NOC. Steven Hao, Cognition’s CTO and the youngest Forbes 400 member at 30 Ilya Pavlov / Unsplash Steven Hao, 30, is No. 1 on Forbes’ 2026 list of the youngest Forbes 400 members, making him the youngest person on the entire ranking. He is worth an estimated $5.8 billion as cofounder and chief technology officer of Cognition, maker of the AI coding agent Devin. Hao comes from the world of competitive programming. He won a gold medal in 2014 at the International Olympiad in Informatics, the top global contest for high school programmers. His two Cognition cofounders, CEO Scott Wu and Walden Yan, are also gold medalists from the same competition. Before Cognition, Hao worked as an engineer at Scale AI, the data labeling startup cofounded by Alexandr Wang. Wang, 29, is a billionaire himself, worth an estimated $3.2 billion, but that falls short of the $4.4 billion needed to make the Forbes 400. Meta $META bought 49% of Scale in 2025. Hao had already left by then to start Cognition in 2023. Cognition introduced Devin in 2024, presenting it as an autonomous AI software engineer that can plan and carry out coding tasks. Devin writes and repairs code for customers that include Citibank and the fintech company Ramp. Cognition expanded in 2025 by acquiring Windsurf, an AI coding tool, after Google $GOOGL hired away Windsurf’s CEO and key staff. The company’s value has climbed quickly. In September 2026, Cognition raised $2 billion at a $48 billion valuation, less than three years after its founding. That round made all three cofounders billionaires. Hao is the largest shareholder among the founders, and he is the only one of the three rich enough to clear the Forbes 400 cutoff. The age range of this year’s Forbes 400 shows how quickly the AI boom has reshaped American wealth. Hao, at 30, is 67 years younger than the list’s oldest member, 97-year-old timber magnate Archie Aldis Emmerson, whose fortune Forbes estimates at $6 billion.

data.title: Companies Are Licensing Workplace Emails, Slack Messages to AI Developers, Often Without Employee Knowledge – NaturalNews.com
data.ai_summary: Companies are licensing internal emails, Slack messages, and documents to AI developers, often without employee knowledge. Payments range from $100,000 to $2 million, and the practice raises consent and privacy concerns. The legal and ethical framework remains unsettled as AI data spending rises.
data.author: Edison Reed

data.full_text:
Companies Are Licensing Workplace Emails, Slack Messages to AI Developers, Often Without Employee Knowledge

Companies are increasingly licensing internal emails, Slack messages and documents to artificial intelligence developers, often without the knowledge of the employees whose communications generate the data, according to reports from Business Insider and the International Business Times [1][2]. AI firms including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta are seeking real-world workplace records to train AI agents capable of performing tasks traditionally handled by employees [2][3]. Companies are increasingly licensing internal emails, Slack messages and documents to artificial intelligence developers, often without the knowledge of the employees whose communications generate the data, according to reports from Business Insider and the International Business Times [1][2]. AI firms including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta are seeking real-world workplace records to train AI agents capable of performing tasks traditionally handled by employees [2][3]. The market has expanded as defunct and struggling companies look to monetize their internal archives, including employee emails, Slack messages and private workplace communications [4][5]. Employees whose communications make up the data may receive no share of the proceeds and may not be informed of the transactions, according to the reports [1][6]. The arrangements have raised questions about consent, privacy law and who profits from workplace records that workers often assume are confidential [1][6]. Brokers Report Growing Demand and Short Decision Windows Brokers approach businesses with archives and offer to buy them, remove sensitive information and license the remaining data to AI developers [2][3]. The size of offers can depend on the volume of information, its exclusivity and the industry involved, according to the report [2][7]. AI companies are buying workplace data including Slack messages, emails, internal documents and tickets to train better models, with payments ranging from $100,000 to $2 million [7]. Spirit Airlines Archive Draws Lawmaker and Employee Concerns Google said it was not seeking personal information and that such data would be excluded or de-identified by an independent third party, according to the reports [2]. Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University, described the question of whether employee consent extends to subsequent sale of data as an "ethically gray area" [2]. The dispute highlights the unresolved question of whether consent to workplace data collection extends to its sale or licensing for AI training [2][6]. Security and Consent Questions Remain Unsettled Nick Heiner, who works on AI training environments at Surge AI, told Business Insider that someone approached him offering a large company's codebase for millions of dollars; he concluded the group did not have the rights to sell it [2]. The account illustrates the legal uncertainty surrounding data provenance in the emerging market [2][6]. Meta faced internal backlash over plans to collect employees' keystrokes and mouse movements for AI training, according to reports [2]. Data intended to be anonymised became accessible more widely within Meta than intended, and the material reportedly included employees' private conversations and performance records [2]. Meta suspended the project following the incident, according to the reports [2]. The episode has been cited by critics as evidence that technical safeguards intended to protect employee data can fail during large-scale AI training efforts [2][6]. Market Growth Continues as Rules Remain Unclear Alex Rosenblat, a sociologist and former Uber policy executive, said growing use of employee records to train AI could intensify calls for stronger privacy protections [2]. The dispute over the Spirit Airlines archive highlights the unresolved question of whether consent to workplace data collection extends to its sale or licensing for AI training [2][6]. As spending on AI data continues to rise, according to Gartner's forecast, the legal and ethical framework governing workplace communications remains unsettled [2]. data.title: Los 10 multimillonarios sub 40 más ricos del mundo: quiénes son y cómo obtuvieron su fortuna
data.ai_summary: Mark Mateschitz, 34, leads the world's richest under-40s with a $29.9 billion fortune from his Red Bull stake. The list includes Greg Brockman, Patrick Collison, and others, with a projected $84 trillion wealth transfer from baby boomers by 2046.
data.author: Agregar Ámbito En
data.full_text:
Mark Mateschitz encabeza el podio de los jóvenes magnates más ricos del planeta, impulsado por el imperio Red Bull. Quiénes son las diez figuras menores de 40 años que sus sectores, en vísperas de la mayor transferencia patrimonial de la historia.

Mark Mateschitz, hijo del fallecido cofundador de la compañía de bebidas energéticas Red Bull , Dietrich Mateschitz, es el multimillonario menor de 40 años más rico del mundo , según el más reciente ranking de millonarios "sub 40". Con 34 años, el heredero austríaco encabeza el ranking con una fortuna estimada en u$s29.900 millones.

Según los datos brindados por la agencia Bloomberg, este es el detalle del top 10 de los multimillonarios menores de 40 años:

Tras heredar el paquete accionario de su padre, Mark Mateschitz se posicionó en el puesto 79 del ranking global de Bloomberg. El joven magnate tiene en su haber el 49% de Red Bull, la firma líder en el mercado mundial de bebidas energéticas que en 2025 vendió 14.000 millones de latas y facturó 12.200 millones de euros.

Detrás de Mateschitz se ubica Greg Brockman , cofundador y presidente de OpenAI, quien con 38 años acumula una fortuna de u$s25.500 millones. La empresa detrás del fenómeno ChatGPT cerró 2025 con ingresos superiores a los u$s20.000 millones, motorizados por el auge del chatbot de IA que en septiembre de 2026 ya superaba los 1.000 millones de usuarios activos por semana.

Tras heredar el paquete accionario de su padre, Mark Mateschitz se posicionó en el puesto 79 del ranking global de Bloomberg.

El tercer lugar del podio pertenece al checo Michal Strnad , de 34 años, cuya fortuna alcanza los u$s18.900 millones. Strnad preside y controla accionariamente Czechoslovak Group (CSG) , un importante conglomerado industrial que fabrica equipos militares y que cerró 2025 con una facturación anual de 6.700 millones de euros.

En el cuarto lugar se ubica Patrick Collison, el irlandés de 38 años que dirige Stripe como cofundador y CEO. Gracias a una tenencia accionaria estimada en el 12% de la firma de pagos digitales —proveedora de gigantes como Amazon, Shopify y Lyft—, su fortuna alcanza los u$s16.300 millones, empatando en partes iguales con el patrimonio de su hermano menor y cofundador, John Collison (36 años).

Detrás de Mateschitz se ubica Greg Brockman, cofundador y presidente de OpenAI, quien con 38 años acumula una fortuna de u$s25.500 millones.

En la sexta posición se ubica el fundador de Surge AI, el estadounidense de raíces taiwanesas Edwin Chen, quien cuenta con un patrimonio actual estimado en u$s13.000 millones. Con sede en San Francisco, su compañía se especializa en la evaluación y el análisis de datos generados por inteligencia artificial para grandes actores del sector tecnológico, tales como OpenAI, Anthropic y Microsoft (MSFT).

Luego, figura el británico Hugh Grosvenor (35 años), con un patrimonio de u$s12.700 millones consolidado en el sector inmobiliario. El aristócrata y duque de Westminster encabeza la empresa inmobiliaria Grosvenor Group, que administra activos por u$s12.800 millones. Asimismo, de acuerdo con los registros de Bloomberg, Grosvenor heredó valiosas extensiones de tierra pertenecientes a su familia desde 1677.

El octavo puesto pertenece al chino Wang Ning (39 años), fundador y CEO de Pop Mart International, quien ostenta un patrimonio de u$s12.100 millones. La firma asiática —famosa por la fabricación de las figuras en cajas sorpresa y los virales muñecos Labubu— está controlada en un 47% por Wang mediante tres sociedades holding, según documentos presentados en junio de 2026.

El tercer lugar del podio pertenece al checo Michal Strnad, de 34 años, cuya fortuna alcanza los u$s18.900 millones.

Más abajo en el listado se ubica el inversor y emprendedor del sector cripto Justin Sun (36 años), originario de China, quien cuenta con un patrimonio estimado en u$s8.180 millones.

El décimo lugar del ranking lo ocupa la estadounidense Daniela Amodei, de 39 años, con un patrimonio de u$s7.980 millones. La empresaria es cofundadora de Anthropic, la firma creadora de los modelos de IA Claude lanzada en 2021 por excolaboradores de OpenAI. De acuerdo con Bloomberg, Amodei controla casi el 1% de las acciones del gigante de la IA.

La transferencia de riqueza

En las próximas dos décadas se desplegará una transferencia histórica de riqueza: se estima que la generación de los baby boomers leguen a nivel global u$s84 billones a sus herederos. Según un reporte de Natixis Investment Managers (Natixis IM), esta masiva reasignación de patrimonio reconfigurará el negocio del asesoramiento financiero y las estrategias de inversión a nivel mundial.

A medida que los primeros integrantes de los 1.100 millones de baby boomers alcanzan los 80 años en 2026, la industria de la asesoría financiera alista una profunda transformación en la que los herederos tomarán el control sobre la gestión del patrimonio heredado, según señala el informe Great Wealth Transfer.

“La gran transferencia de patrimonio supone un reto clave para los asesores, por lo que será fundamental adaptarse a las preferencias de los nuevos herederos”, sostuvo Andrew Benton, director de Natixis IM para el norte de Europa, Medio Oriente y África.

En el cuarto lugar se ubica Patrick Collison, el irlandés de 38 años que dirige Stripe como cofundador y CEO. Dirige la empresa junto a su hermano menor John Collison.

A medida que los activos cambian de manos, Andrew Benton explica que será imprescindible reevaluar los perfiles de riesgo y las preferencias de inversión, considerando las marcadas diferencias en la visión estratégica de cada generación.

En general, los jóvenes de la generación millennial (de 30 a 45 años) se posicionan como el perfil menos conservador. De acuerdo con la encuesta de Natixis, un 75% manifiesta su deseo de superar el rendimiento del mercado. A nivel global, este segmento muestra una fuerte inclinación por los activos privados (55%), al tiempo que un 46% ya invierte directamente en criptomonedas.

data.title: Companies Are Selling Employees' Private Slack Messages and Emails to Train AI—Often Without Workers' Knowledge
data.ai_summary: Companies are licensing employees' private emails and Slack messages to AI developers, often without workers' knowledge. Offers can be six-figure deals with 48-hour deadlines, and Google's $10 million purchase of Spirit Airlines' data has raised privacy concerns. The practice raises questions about employee consent and data ownership.
data.author: Regyl Jaen

industries.name: Ethical Data Sourcing, Consent & Data Provenance
AI Privacy Engineering & Data Governance (PII, consent, retention)

data.full_text:
Companies Are Selling Employees' Private Slack Messages and Emails to Train AI—Often Without Workers' Knowledge
As corporate data changes hands, workers face a troubling question: Who really owns their digital footprints?
Companies are increasingly licensing workplace emails, Slack messages, and internal documents to AI developers, creating a lucrative market that some employees may not know about. As AI firms race to automate office jobs, businesses are receiving six-figure offers for their digital records, sometimes with just 48 hours to decide.
These deals can generate substantial revenue, but they also raise questions about employee privacy, consent, and who should benefit financially from the information workers create. 'Right now, the demand is just astronomical,' said Dan Novaes, chief executive of data broker Mode.Inc., speaking to Business Insider.
Business Data Has Become the New Oil
AI developers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta, are seeking real-world workplace records to train AI agents capable of performing tasks traditionally handled by employees. Gartner's September 2026 forecast confirms that worldwide spending on AI data is projected to reach $6.48 billion in 2027, reflecting growing demand for data used in AI development.
Brokers approach businesses with extensive archives, offering to buy their records, remove sensitive information, and license the remaining data to AI developers. Offers can depend on the volume of information, its exclusivity, and the industry involved.
Ryan Lock, co-founder of AI data broker Polyshares, compared the practice to early oil prospectors who bought land from farmers unaware of the oil beneath it. 'The offers being made look almost identical to those early oil offers,' he said. 'They'll say, "I'm offering you double market. I need an answer by Friday."'
Employees, meanwhile, may receive no share of the proceeds, despite generating the emails, presentations, and internal conversations that make the data valuable. Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University, described the question of whether employees' consent extends to the subsequent sale of their data as an 'ethically gray area'.
Spirit Airlines Data Deal Raises Employee Privacy Concerns
The risks extend beyond active businesses. Google's proposed $10 million purchase of internal Spirit Airlines data has raised concerns among former employees and lawmakers. The airline, which ceased operations in May 2026, had an archive containing approximately 100 million emails and 500 million Microsoft Teams messages.
On 8 October, more than 120 US lawmakers, led by Senator Elizabeth Warren and Representative Steven Horsford, urged Google and Spirit Airlines to protect former employees' privacy in connection with the proposed $10 million data deal. Google said it was not seeking personal information and that such data would be excluded or de-identified by an independent third party, according to reports.
The dispute highlights a difficult question: does an employee's consent to workplace data collection also extend to the subsequent sale or licensing of that data for AI training?
Data Access and Security Add to Privacy Fears
The risks are not limited to legitimate data sales. Nick Heiner, who works on AI training environments at Surge AI, told Business Insider that someone had approached him offering a large company's codebase for millions of dollars. He concluded the group did not have the rights to sell it.
Meta has also faced internal backlash over plans to collect employees' keystrokes and mouse movements for AI training. The initiative raised fears that sensitive information could be captured. According to reports, data intended to be anonymised became accessible more widely within Meta than intended. The material reportedly included employees' private conversations and performance records. Meta suspended the project following the incident.
A Growing Market With Unsettled Rules
The growing use of employee records to train AI could intensify calls for stronger privacy protections, said Alex Rosenblat, a sociologist and former Uber policy executive. It could also give employees new leverage and negotiating power as the value of their everyday digital footprint grows, she said.
'It's not that data collection wasn't present before; it's that the scale at which it can happen, the scale at which it is useful, has shifted,' Rosenblat said. 'And that's an opportunity for people to say, "wait a minute, the value of this is escaping us."'

data.title: Who Is Building Ground Truth for AI Agents? Top 5 best companies
data.ai_summary: Five companies—Scale AI, Keymakr, Surge AI, Labelbox, and Appen—are profiled as providers of ground truth data for AI agents. Each offers specialized platforms for labeling, RLHF, and evaluation, with Scale AI and Appen noted for large-scale projects. The article emphasizes that ground truth quality determines agent performance.
data.author: Balla

industries.name: RLHF, Human Feedback & Evaluation Data Tools
Data Quality, Validation & Ground Truth Auditing

data.full_text:
As AI agents become increasingly complex, the importance of the high-quality data they are trained on grows as well. Modern agentic systems require high-precision ground truth datasets, human feedback, response evaluation, chains of thought, and data for RLHF. This is exactly why companies engaged in data preparation and validation have become key elements of the AI ecosystem. What to look for when choosing a data provider? Before choosing a ground truth provider for AI agents, several factors should be evaluated: Quality control and verification – a reliable QA technology that combines automated algorithmic checks with multi-level human auditing.

Availability of subject matter experts – complex AI systems can only be created by people with relevant expertise.

Support for RLHF and model evaluation – modern models heavily rely on human feedback and evaluation.

Tools and integration – the ability to process large volumes of data and work with multiple languages and data types.

Security and compliance – strict adherence to GDPR, ISO/IEC 27001, and SOC 2 standards, especially if agents will work with confidential corporate data.

A combination of human expertise and automation allows maintaining both quality and speed simultaneously. Top 5 companies building ground truth for AI agents 1. Scale AI One of the most prominent giants of the industry and a key partner for leading AI laboratories (OpenAI, Meta, Microsoft). The company has built a massive ecosystem for generative AI, LLMs, autonomous systems, and next-generation agents. In addition to classic labeling, they specialize in RLHF, model testing, performance evaluation, and AI safety. Thanks to its colossal infrastructure, the company can support large-scale, ultra-complex projects. The company has its own Scale GenAI platform and a network of subject-matter experts who provide reinforcement learning and model evaluation services at an industrial scale. Best suited for: large AI companies that need millions of volumes of high-quality textual and multimodal data within tight deadlines. 2. Keymakr The company has made a powerful leap forward by offering targeted solutions specifically for agentic AI, computer vision, NLP, and complex autonomous systems. Instead of scattering efforts across standard mass labeling, they combine high-precision manual annotation from their in-house team with automated quality-control tools. A flexible approach and the ability to work with custom requirements make the company attractive to both startups and enterprise clients. Their own Keylabs platform is a powerful proprietary enterprise solution for image, video, and 3D data annotation with integrated ML automation algorithms, annotator action tracking, and multi-level QA management. They involve subject matter experts to write complex chains of thought and deploy them in RLHF. Best suited for: custom AI projects, computer vision, multimodal agents, developers of deep research systems, and robotics. 3. Surge AI A company that shifted the focus from quantity to the flawless quality of human feedback. It focuses on creating datasets for complex tasks related to logical reasoning, security, and model alignment. Thanks to this, Surge AI has become one of the key players in the field of data preparation for modern LLMs and AI agents that must operate with nuances of language and context. The platform utilizes a unique framework for adversarial testing, allowing humans to intentionally “break” models to identify vulnerabilities, alongside automated LLM-based QC bots to verify human labeling. Best suited for: RLHF tasks, building reasoning datasets, alignment tasks, and deep model evaluation. 4. Labelbox This provider offers complex software to the market. Labelbox positions itself as a full-fledged data management platform, providing clients with tools for dataset preparation, process automation, model evaluation, and the organization of human feedback within a single interface. The Labelbox platform includes modules for data management, labeling, and testing & evaluation. It allows companies to centralize their data operations. Instead of simply buying a ready-made dataset, teams get an environment where they can automate labeling with their own models and flexibly integrate both internal annotators and external crowdsourced workers. Best suited for: teams and companies seeking full control and tools to manage the entire data lifecycle and build their own AI infrastructure. 5. Appen One of the oldest, largest, and most experienced players in the global AI data market. The company’s main advantage is a colossal global network of contributors and support for hundreds of languages and dialects, allowing it to collect and annotate large-scale multilingual text, audio, and visual datasets. The Appen platform automates task distribution and quality control across a network of millions of contributors. It offers the capability to scale rapidly in geography and language. For AI agent developers, this means access to ground truth data that accounts for local cultural contexts, speech specifics, and local regulatory requirements. Best suited for: large-scale data collection, AI localization, and large multilingual projects for international markets. Who holds the keys to the autonomous future? The irony of artificial intelligence development is that the more autonomous AI agents become, the more heavily they depend on humans during their formative stage. We attempt to delegate complex work to machines – from managing investment portfolios to performing surgical operations – but the safety of this transition rests entirely on the shoulders of ground truth providers. The companies we reviewed today are literally writing the rules of the game by which the global digital economy will live tomorrow. When building your own AI agent, it is essential to consider that while the model architecture or algorithms represent the car’s chassis, the ground truth is its fuel, engine, and roadmap. And the cleanliness and expertise of this fuel will determine whether your agent reaches its destination or spins out on the very first sharp turn of the real world. Author: Balla

data.title: AI labs are offering companies big money to hand over their employees' private Slack DMs and emails
data.ai_summary: AI labs are offering companies six-figure deals to sell their employees' private Slack DMs and emails, with offers expiring in 48 hours. The market is projected to grow from under $1 billion last year to nearly $6.5 billion in 2027, and some companies like Springshot were blindsided by Google's purchase. The lack of federal privacy laws leaves few legal barriers.
data.author: Charles Rollet; Tom Carter; Stephen Council

industries.name: Ethical Data Sourcing, Consent & Data Provenance

data.full_text:
As they race to automate white-collar work, AI labs have found the perfect source of training data: your Slack DMs.
Business owners are getting six-figure "exploding offers" that expire in 48 hours to sell their data. Instagram is flooded with ads declaring that "AI needs your data" and promising millions. The data is priced by the terabyte, anonymized, and sold to AI giants desperate for an edge.
Tech giants have moved to harvest their employees' data for AI training. And, once focused on dead startups, brokers now pay for live data from active companies.
"Right now, the demand is just astronomical," said Dan Novaes, the CEO of Mode.Inc, a startup that sells data to AI model developers.
Mundane workplace data is more valuable than ever as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and others build AI agents for businesses. Annual spending on data for AI is projected to explode from less than $1 billion last year to almost $6.5 billion in 2027, Gartner estimates.
The boom has a darker side. Employees rarely profit from — or know about — their Slacks, PowerPoints, and Google Docs being sold to the highest bidder. Suspected hackers have shopped around a large company's stolen codebase for millions of dollars. Meta's attempt to harvest its own employees' data for its AI models sparked a revolt.
Some CEOs are getting blindsided. Doug Kreuzkamp, who runs airline operations company Springshot, was sitting in his office on a Zoom call in August when he found out that Google had bought his data. Springshot, a longtime vendor for the now-bankrupt Spirit Airlines, helped flights coordinate with workers such as gate agents and cleaners.
"I had less than 48 hours' notice — from the media — that the intellectual property we had spent 15 years building could be given away," Kreuzkamp told Business Insider.
The surging market is pushing into uncharted waters, and the industry risks a reckoning with workers and regulators, said Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University. The lack of federal privacy laws leaves few legal barriers to companies collecting data from their employees for AI training, she added.
"The question is, does the consent of the employees from whom they collected that data actually extend to the sale of the data? I think it's an ethically gray area," Ajunwa said.
Business data has become the new oil
The boom has created a thriving group of go-betweens who hunt for small businesses rich in data and low on cash. After scrubbing sensitive information like Social Security numbers and home addresses, they resell it to AI giants.
Although the industry is new, it's become highly competitive. Ryan Lock, cofounder of AI broker Polyshares, compares it to the oil boom that hit Texas in the early 1900s, when prospectors snapped up cheap land from farmers who didn't realize the true value of the oil underneath it.
Small-business owners sitting on troves of internal records may not realize the seemingly mundane files could be worth big money. Tactics like 48-hour deadlines have become common, Lock said.
"The offers being made look almost identical to those early oil offers," he said from his home base in Dallas. "They'll say, 'I'm offering you double market. I need an answer by Friday.'"
Lock and his cofounders went through the data-licensing process themselves with their other companies, sometimes laughing out loud at the lowball offers they got. Their firm tries to bridge that information gap by giving business owners more transparency about what their data is worth.
"There's still plenty of money for everyone, but business owners should receive more of the benefit," he said.
Wanted: data from companies, dead or alive
Data that demonstrates how work is actually done is highly valuable, said William Almeida, the chief revenue officer of AI training startup Micro1, because it provides critical context on how decisions are made and products are built.
That information can help train agents, the autonomous computer-using AI tools that have become a major focus for companies like Meta and SpaceXAI. As AI companies build new models, the real-world data guides the AI on how best to handle specific tasks.
Micro1 announced a program earlier this year that pays midsize companies $100,000 to $2 million for access to anonymized data. Almeida said AI developers increasingly want "long-horizon" data that can provide a full picture of how work gets done. If a company won't sell its Slack, customer relationship management, or email records, the rest of the corpus is less valuable.
The data is priced based on a multitude of factors, with volume being a critical one. The more white-collar employees a company has, the more valuable its data corpus is, said Novaes, the Mode.Inc CEO.
Other factors, like exclusivity, matter — there's lower demand for a codebase that a rival lab already has its hands on. Fields that AI giants are trying the hardest to automate, like law and accounting, see especially high demand.
Generally, though, any company — dead or alive, big or small — can sell its data, as long as it has enough.
"People need to wake up to it and take this opportunity," Novaes said.
Grant Gooley decided to license his company's data to an AI training company. His agency, MyPortal Marketing, has sold Micro1 everything from Figma and Canva files to checklists for onboarding clients to Google ads. He said it didn't sell client-specific material.
"If AI is going to be trained, why not be part of that, and do it responsibly?" Gooley said.
A new breed of security and privacy concerns
While the market creates wealth for some, it's breeding new kinds of cybersecurity and privacy risks for others.
Nick Heiner helps improve AI agents by building office-like digital environments at AI training startup Surge AI. Heiner said that earlier this year, he was approached by a group offering a large company's codebase for millions of dollars.
"It became apparent that this group did not have the rights to sell this data," Heiner told Business Insider. "They had illicitly obtained a copy of the codebase and were just going around to all the data vendors saying, 'Can I get a few million bucks for this?'"
Security and consent concerns aren't limited to hackers. Google's bid to buy Spirit Airlines' old data for $10 million has been held up, in part, by flight attendants worried about how their records will be used. Last week, Sen. Elizabeth Warren and over 100 other members of Congress wrote a letter to Google and Spirit urging the companies to protect the privacy of thousands of former Spirit employees.
A Google spokesperson told Business Insider that it's not looking to buy any personal information from Spirit Airlines and that any such data would be either excluded or de-identified by an independent third party. A representative for Spirit said the company is working closely with the flight attendants and other unions to address their concerns.
Former gig workers for Mercor, another AI training startup, have alleged in an ongoing lawsuit that the company encouraged them to upload work materials without their employers' consent. Mercor has denied their claims in court.
The hunger for work records is so strong that some tech giants have tried tracking their own staff.
At Meta, employees revolted when the company announced a new program earlier this year to track their keystrokes and mouse movements for AI training. Employees worried that Meta would capture their sensitive data, like credit card numbers and immigration documents.
Although Meta's chief technology officer, Andrew Bosworth, pledged that the data would be "tightly controlled," it turned out that it had been viewable across the company in a major internal leak. The supposedly anonymized data included employees' private conversations and performance records, screenshots obtained by Business Insider show. Meta suspended the project shortly after the breach and hasn't restarted it.
Google once considered tracking its staff's AI output and ultimately dropped the idea, Business Insider previously reported.
The Meta revolt hasn't stopped other companies from eyeing employee data as a useful shortcut to AI domination, including the world's richest man.
In an all-hands meeting in August, CEO Elon Musk told employees that SpaceX would train its Grok AI on worker data and encouraged them to think of themselves as the model's "parents."
"In a way, it will be trained on you. It will inherit your thoughts and ideas and beliefs, and I think that's a good thing," Musk said.
A huge market that few workers are aware of
Though the company data market is nascent, the AI training startups cashing in are optimistic.
Ali Ansari, Micro1's CEO, says licensing data to labs could become one of the most common revenue sources for businesses worldwide, he recently posted on X. He estimates that, soon, about 10% of the US's GDP could be dedicated to training AI models, thanks to business data and human professionals.
Last week, Micro1 announced a commitment to spend $1 billion on company data over the next 12 months.
The growing use of employee records for AI training could heighten the urgency of calls for new data protection and privacy regulations, said Alex Rosenblat, a sociologist and former Uber policy executive.
It could also give employees new leverage and negotiating power as the value of their everyday digital footprint grows, she said.
"It's not that data collection wasn't present before; it's that the scale at which it can happen, the scale at which it is useful, has shifted," Rosenblat said.
"And that's an opportunity for people to say, 'wait a minute, the value of this is escaping us.'"

data.title: AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models
data.ai_summary: SimpleClosure, a startup-wind-down firm, now sells code and workspace data to AI labs, having handled over 150 deals. Buyers include foundation AI labs and vendors, with deals expected to return over $10 million to startups by 2026. Legal concerns about privacy and fair pricing remain.
data.author: Matthew Kingarchive Page
data.full_text: When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup this year, he didn’t think its data was worth much: the users were anonymous, the company just a few years old. But he’s since turned the firm’s digital archives into real money. He’s netted roughly $25,000 for his code base and a still-pending amount (likely around $15,000) for the workspace data in Google, Notion, Figma, and Slack. “At least all that stuff we were doing for two and a half years is worth something to someone somewhere,” he says. The sale was brokered by a company called SimpleClosure, part of a new growth sector in tech: businesses catering to dying startups. Estimates from Carta and AngelList show shutdowns rising between 26% and 56% annually in recent years, and an end-of-life ecosystem—including coaches, “death doulas,” and firms that help handle the legal, tax, and operational headaches of going ­belly-up—has emerged. Now tech undertakers are selling the data remains to AI labs. Related Story A major AI training data set contains millions of examples of personal data Read next SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April. Its Asset Hub platform helps founders sell their code and workspace data—emails, chats, documents. Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that construct simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models. Asset Hub has handled over 150 deals and expects to return over $10 million to startups by the end of 2026. CEO Dori Yona has seen these transactions, once rare and “somewhat taboo,” become increasingly routine, with 47% of SimpleClosure deals now including code or data sales. And it’s got company. Industry rival Sunset also has a rapidly growing data resale business. Founder and CEO Brendan Mahony says Sunset values a dying client’s assets by head count, years in operation, volume of data, and how the team used its tools. Particle board, he says, is a good analogy: “This operational exhaust data is like the wood shavings that everyone thought had no value, but it actually has a ton.” Demand for defunct companies’ data emerged suddenly last year, as AI training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets. Surge AI, for example, buys data to build “reinforcement-learning gyms” where clients’ AI agents practice tasks—think debugging a complex IT architecture or drafting appellate briefs. Nick Heiner, who leads the company’s work on these environments, says he seeks data archives reflecting a range of situations, from disagreements to tricky judgment calls. Heiner explains that one company’s Slack history, if it captures conversations with variety and depth, can be worth more than another’s Slack, email, and calendars combined. Real archives avoid common errors in synthetic worlds, such as references to dates that don’t exist, but the extent of performance gains remains unclear. No company has yet released tests comparing results of real-world data training with the alternatives. Pricing reflects this uncertainty: Buyers quote wildly different numbers, Heiner says, because valuations are based on “research theses” estimating how many useful tasks come from, say, 100,000 lines of code. That hasn’t stopped bigger deals from happening. This past August, as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy, Google outbid the AI data company Mercor to buy the carrier’s decades of data, including 100 million emails, 500 million Teams messages, and 176,000 employee records. The price tag: $10 million. And Bloomberg reported in September that SpaceX’s AI unit is weighing buying data from struggling startups. Legally, this all could get iffy. Spirit’s flight attendants’ union objected to the sale on privacy grounds, and Greg Ewing, an attorney who advises AI startups, has called such data “legally radioactive.” Suppliers employ data scientists to scrub personally identifiable information and exclude HR records, and buyers say they scrub too. But Ewing points out some of the private details that lurk in emails and calendars: doctor appointments, school pickup arrangements, date-night plans. He describes a “Wild West of AI training” that is only starting to give way to proper licensing agreements and vetted use. There’s also the question of who profits from these windfalls. The proceeds typically flow to senior creditors and investors—not employees. To Ifeoma Ajunwa, a law professor at Emory University and author of The Quantified Worker, this represents a form of “captured capital.” Legal precedent allows for monitoring to help workers do their jobs, but once a firm is out of business, that justification vanishes. “Employers should have express consent before selling workers’ data,” says Ajunwa, but she adds that there’s no federal law banning such sales. While many see this new market as a chance for failing businesses to recover some value, these wind-down sales also have limitations. Founders have little to no visibility into who is buying the data and what they plan to do with it. Plus, there’s little assurance they’re getting a fair offer. Data prices will likely stabilize in the coming year, though, unless an AI bubble pops first. Either way, tech’s new undertakers will be there to appraise what’s left. Matthew King is a technology and environmental journalist based in Baltimore.

data.title: Así está el listado de los multimillonarios estadounidenses más jóvenes
data.ai_summary: The Forbes 400 2026 lists the youngest billionaires, with net worths from $5.8B to $44.4B, including Steven Hao at $5.8B. Eight of the ten youngest are tied to private AI companies, with Anthropic holding four of them.
data.author: Editorial La República S.A.S.
data.full_text:
La lista Forbes 400 de 2026 incluye entre sus integrantes más jóvenes a empresarios vinculados a compañías como OpenAI, Surge AI, Anthropic y Cognition

La inteligencia artificial no solo está impulsando algunas de las empresas emergentes más valiosas de Estados Unidos, sino que también está dando paso a una nueva generación de multimillonarios. La lista Forbes 400 de 2026 incluye entre sus integrantes más jóvenes a fundadores y ejecutivos vinculados con compañías como OpenAI, Surge AI, Anthropic y Cognition. De acuerdo con los datos, las fortunas de los 10 integrantes más jóvenes de la lista van desde US$5.800 millones hasta US$44.400 millones. Las estimaciones corresponden al 4 de septiembre de 2026, mientras que el patrimonio mínimo requerido para formar parte de la Forbes 400 de este año fue de US$4.400 millones. El integrante más joven es Steven Hao, de 30 años, con un patrimonio estimado de US$5.800 millones, asociado a Cognition. Le sigue Palmer Luckey, de 33 años, fundador de Anduril, con US$5.900 millones. Sam McCandlish, de 36 años, y Jack Clark, de 37, aparecen con US$15.500 millones cada uno, vinculados a Anthropic. Con 38 años, Greg Brockman, de OpenAI, registra un patrimonio de US$25.500 millones, mientras que Edwin Chen, fundador de Surge AI, alcanza US$18.000 millones. Entre los integrantes de 39 años aparecen Lukas Walton, con US$44.400 millones; Daniela Amodei y Tom Brown, con US$15.500 millones cada uno; y Vlad Tenev, de Robinhood, con US$7.100 millones. La clasificación también muestra el peso de las empresas privadas en la creación de estas fortunas. Ocho de las diez riquezas incluidas se basan en participaciones en compañías privadas, cuyas valoraciones se calculan a partir de rondas de financiación recientes. A diferencia de las compañías que cotizan en bolsa, las empresas privadas no cuentan con un precio de mercado que se actualice continuamente. Por ello, una nueva ronda de financiación puede modificar la valoración de una compañía y, en consecuencia, alterar de manera significativa la estimación del patrimonio de sus principales accionistas. Entre las compañías de inteligencia artificial presentes en esta lista se encuentran OpenAI, Surge AI, Anthropic y Cognition. El caso de Anthropic destaca por concentrar a cuatro de los 10 integrantes: Sam McCandlish, Jack Clark, Daniela Amodei y Tom Brown, todos con patrimonios estimados en US$15.500 millones.

data.title: AI Training-Data Startup Micro1 Reportedly Hits $4B Valuation
data.ai_summary: Micro1 raised over $100 million at a $4 billion valuation, an eightfold jump from its $500 million valuation in September 2025. The San Francisco startup's annualized revenue grew from $7 million in early 2025 to over $500 million, with net revenue estimated at $150-200 million.
data.author: 버섯돌이 Taehyun Kim
data.full_text:
The AI training-data market that Scale AI once defined was upended last June. Meta invested $14.3 billion in Scale AI and hired away founder Alexander Wang, and OpenAI and Google — both major Scale AI customers — began pulling back, saying they needed neutral data partners. Among the challengers racing to fill that gap, none has climbed faster than Micro1.

Learn AI Tools

The San Francisco-based startup connects AI labs with domain experts — doctors, lawyers, software engineers — to produce the high-quality human data needed to train frontier models. Its in-house AI interviewer, Zara, screens and vets every candidate before they join the network. Micro1’s customer list includes frontier AI labs along with Microsoft, Amazon, and robotics firm 1X. The company has also been expanding into synthetic data that doesn’t require human involvement, selling the same “off-the-shelf” datasets to multiple customers at gross margins reportedly as high as 80-90%. That practice has drawn criticism for potentially helping Chinese AI developers catch up; founder Ali Ansari has said publicly that Micro1 doesn’t sell its data to Chinese model makers.

Micro1 was founded by Ali Ansari, who started his first venture at age 12. He built software agency moontek while at UC Berkeley, which became the foundation for Micro1. The company began as an engineering-recruitment business before pivoting entirely to supplying frontier AI labs with high-quality human data.

Discover more Find Recruiters Try Office Apps Open Biz Account

According to multiple media reports, Micro1 has recently raised more than $100 million at a $4 billion valuation. That’s an eightfold jump from the $500 million valuation it reached with a $35 million Series A in September 2025. Two frontier AI labs that are also Micro1 customers, along with two co-founders of xAI, reportedly participated as individual investors in the round. Neither Micro1 nor the investors have made an official announcement.

Learn AI Tools

The growth numbers back up the valuation jump. Micro1’s annualized revenue grew from $7 million in early 2025 to more than $500 million today. According to TechCrunch, gross annualized run rate alone jumped from $100 million to $500 million between December and August — an eight-month span — though net revenue, after the roughly 60-70% paid out to contracted experts, is estimated at $150-200 million.

Competition keeps intensifying. Mercor, which raised $350 million at a $10 billion valuation last October, has since crossed $2 billion in gross annualized revenue this summer to cement its decacorn status. Bootstrapped Surge AI posted $1.4 billion in revenue in 2025 and, per Bloomberg, is reportedly pursuing its first-ever outside funding — $1 billion at a $25 billion valuation — though that hasn’t been confirmed. Malaysia’s sovereign wealth fund backed Turing, now valued at $2.2 billion. And Handshake, which refounded itself from a college recruiting platform into an AI data supplier, has topped $1.1 billion in gross annualized revenue.

data.title: ZeroDrift Launches Anchor 3.0, the First Family of Models Built for Enforcement Runtime of AI Agent Communications
data.ai_summary: ZeroDrift announced general availability of Anchor 3.0, small language models for enforcing regulatory rules on AI communications. The models caught 95.5% of violations, outperforming frontier models, and run up to 34x faster and 12x cheaper. Developers can use them today.
data.author: Globe Newswire

industries.name: LLM/GenAI Guardrails & Safety Controls (policy, filtering, routing)

data.full_text:
Anchor 3.0’s purpose-built small language models caught more FINRA violations than every frontier model tested while running up to 34x faster and up to 12x cheaper; generally available to developers today ZeroDrift, the Enforcement Runtime for AI, announced the general availability of Anchor 3.0, the first family of small language models built to enforce regulatory and company rules on AI-generated communications before they’re sent. The company also published the first benchmark measuring how well AI models enforce FINRA rules on business communications, built on human-written, attorney-labeled data independently produced by Surge AI, the data labeling company trusted by the world’s leading AI labs. Anchor 3.0 caught 95.5% of violations, more than any frontier model tested. It also outperformed GPT-5.6 Sol, the strongest frontier model on the test, on recall, precision and F1 — a measure that balances recall and precision — while running up to 34x faster and up to 12x cheaper. Developers can sign up and start using Anchor 3.0 today. Financial institutions are already moving AI from experimentation into production. Cambridge research found that 81% of surveyed financial services firms are adopting AI at some level, with traditional financial institutions reporting 45% agentic AI adoption. FINRA’s 2026 oversight report notes that generative AI can implicate supervision, communications, record-keeping, and fair dealing obligations, and regulators have levied billions of dollars in fines for communications failures. Frontier models can catch many violations, but at 12 to 51 seconds per message for the strongest of them, they can only review after the fact. Anchor 3.0 runs the check on every message before it leaves, in about 1.5 seconds on ZeroDrift’s API and under 100 milliseconds self-hosted. Marketing Technology News: MarTech Interview with Mark Listes, CEO @ Pendulum Intelligence “Frontier models made it easy to build capable agents. The hard part is running them inside a regulated business, where every message has to follow the rules and the check has to happen every time, before anything goes out,” said Kumesh Aroomoogan, founder and CEO of ZeroDrift. “A frontier model is too slow and too expensive to do that on every message. Anchor is built for exactly this job. Developers keep building with the models they choose, and Anchor makes sure what their agents say is compliant.” Anchor 3.0 is available in three sizes: Anchor 3.0 Mini — 9B parameters (4B active), post-trained from Gemma E4B. The fastest and lowest-cost model in the family, built for the highest-volume AI traffic. Runs ZeroDrift’s pre-built rule packs and flags violations.

data.title: Here are 10 of the youngest billionaires in the US — and how they got their fortunes
data.ai_summary: Forbes' annual list of America's 400 richest billionaires shows 10 under 40, up from four last year, with most not inheriting wealth. Seven of them are AI founders, including Anthropic's seven cofounders, while Lukas Walton is the only one inheriting from a family fortune.
data.author: Tristin Hoffman
data.full_text:
New money is in for America's young and rich.
Forbes released its annual list of America's 400 richest billionaires in September, and a record $4.4 billion net worth was required to make the cut.
Just 10 of those billionaires are under 40, up from four on last year's list. And most of them didn't inherit their wealth. The majority of the US' youngest Forbes 400 billionaires — seven of them — got their money from the AI boom as founders.
Of those seven, four come from one company: Anthropic, the AI company founded only five years ago and now valued at $1.5 trillion in the secondary market. Anthropic's seven cofounders all vowed earlier this year to donate 80% of their personal wealth to philanthropic causes.
The other three are founders of Surge AI, OpenAI, and Cognition.
Only one billionaire on the list — Lukas Walton — inherited their wealth from a family fortune. Walton is the grandson of Walmart founder Sam Walton and is also one of two young billionaires who do not live in California. The other, Edwin Chen, lives in New York.
Here are the 10 youngest billionaires in the US.
Lukas Walton
Age: 39
Net worth: $44.4 billion
State: Illinois
Lukas Walton, Illinois' richest person, also runs an impact-investing group called Builders Vision and is chair of the Walton Family Foundation's environment program committee.
As of 2024, Walton has donated at least $150 million of his own fortune to his family's environmental program foundation.
After his father, John T. Walton, died in a plane crash in 2005, Lukas inherited roughly a third of his fortune. Forbes' data shows that the Walton family has a combined net worth of $475.6 billion.
Tom Brown
Age: 39
Net worth: $15.5 billion
State: California
Tom Brown is one of Anthropic's seven cofounders and serves as the company's chief compute officer.
He recently mediated Anthropic's standoff with the US over Claude's AI models Fable 5 and Mythos 5. Claude is Anthropic's conversational AI assistant.
Before Anthropic, Brown worked at OpenAI as a research engineering lead and helped introduce the company's GPT-3 language model.
Brown graduated from MIT in 2010, having studied computer science and cognitive science. He cofounded his first company, social club Grouper, in 2011.
Daniela Amodei
Age: 39
Net worth: $15.5 billion
State: California
Daniela Amodei is Anthropic's president and board chair.
Amodei, like Brown, left her job at OpenAI in 2021 alongside her brother, Dario, to found Anthropic.
Amodei also worked at Stripe, the financial services company, and graduated from UC Santa Cruz in 2009 with a B.A. in English Literature and a minor in politics.
She's previously stated that she doesn't regret her college major, arguing that artificial intelligence will only increase the importance of humanities majors.
"The ability to have critical thinking skills will be more important in the future, rather than less," she said in an interview earlier this year.
Vlad Tenev
Age: 39
Net worth: $7.1 billion
State: California
Vlad Tenev, who was born in Bulgaria, co-founded stock trading app Robinhood in 2013 with Stanford colleague Baiju Bhatt, who is also on Forbes' 400 list this year.
Robinhood went public in 2021 and is now leaning much of its business toward prediction markets, where participants buy and sell contracts on future events related to the weather, sports, elections, Federal Reserve decisions, and more.
The company has a market cap of $107.7 billion. According to Forbes, Tenev owns about 6% of the company.
Tenev is also the cofounder and executive chairman of Harmonic, which builds AI systems that excel at advanced mathematical reasoning.
Edwin Chen
Age: 38
Net worth: $18 billion
State: New York
Chen is the founder of Surge AI, a data labeling and AI training company with an annual revenue exceeding $1 billion. Chen owns about 75% of the company and counts customers such as Google and Anthropic.
He is an MIT graduate, having studied math, linguistics, and computer science. Before founding Surge AI in 2020, he worked at Google, Facebook, and Twitter.
He is the son of Taiwanese immigrants and is from Florida.
Greg Brockman
Age: 37
Net worth: $25.5 billion
State: California
Greg Brockman is a Harvard and MIT dropout.
Before completing his studies, he traded in schoolwork for the role of Stripe's chief technology officer at 25.
Three years later, in 2015, Brockman cofounded OpenAI alongside Elon Musk and Sam Altman. He currently serves as the company's president, overseeing its models' infrastructure.
His stake in the company is nearly $30 billion, he said earlier this year.
Jack Clark
Age: 37
Net worth: $15.5 billion
State: California
Jack Clark was first a Bloomberg reporter covering artificial intelligence before becoming one of the industry's best-known founders.
Clark joined OpenAI as its policy director in 2016. Five years later, he cofounded Anthropic and now runs the company's in-house think tank operations, studying AI's effects on society.
He is a widely respected advisor on AI safety, and also writes the email newsletter "Import AI," which many field researchers follow. Clark has coauthored several AI research papers.
Sam McCandlish
Age: 36
Net worth: $15.5 billion
State: California
Sam McCandlish is another Anthropic cofounder who first worked at OpenAI.
There, he worked on scaling laws, the idea that AI systems become more capable as they are trained with more data and computing power.
Now, as chief architect at Anthropic, he oversees how its models are built and trained. He previously served as Anthropic's chief technology officer.
McCandlish earned a Ph.D. in theoretical physics from Stanford in 2017.
Palmer Luckey
Age: 33
Net worth: $5.9 billion
State: California
Palmer Luckey got his career head start as a teenager when he built a virtual reality headset and, in 2012, founded a company to sell it. He sold the company, Oculus, to Meta two years later for $2 billion in cash and stock.
Meta fired Luckey in 2016 after he made a political contribution to a pro-Donald Trump group. Meta denied that his departure had anything to do with his politics.
Since then, Luckey co-founded Anduril, a defense-tech company that builds AI software and autonomous military hardware. As of May, the company is valued at $61 billion.
Steven Hao
Age: 30
Net worth: $5.8 billion
State: California
Steven Hao, the youngest billionaire in the US, left Scale AI, a data-labeling startup, to found Cognition in 2023.
Cognition makes AI software that writes and repairs code. Its customers include Citibank and fintech Ramp, and the company is valued at $48 billion.
Hao, alongside fellow cofounders Scott Wu and Walden Yan, is a former competitive programmer, having won a gold medal at the International Olympiad in Informatics, the global competitive programming championship.
